key_insight: Multi-agent LLM scaling depends strongly on task structure: disjunctive tasks benefit from larger teams only in principle, while compensatory tasks like Fermi estimation are dominated by shared model bias and gain little from averaging.
engineering_relevance: When designing multi-agent systems, the aggregation rule and task type matter as much as team size, so simply adding more agents is not a reliable path to better performance.
method: Introduced Steiner’s taxonomy of group tasks to analyze multi-agent LLM scaling, focusing on disjunctive and compensatory tasks.
Modeled agents as conditionally independent given the item to derive large-team limits for plurality voting and averaging.
Evaluated 13 open-weight models on representative benchmarks with teams up to 30 agents.
evidence_signal: Across benchmarks, the chance that at least one agent is correct rose by 5–20 points with team size on disjunctive tasks, but plurality voting captured almost none of that potential; for Fermi estimation, item-level bias explained about 87% of squared error and averaging reduced error by only about 6%.
watch_item: The reported gains are benchmark- and aggregation-dependent, so results may not transfer to tasks with different dependence structures, prompting, or stronger cross-agent diversity.
paper_title: Multi-agent Scaling Across Disjunctive and Compensatory Tasks
